\section*{Question 3}

The figure above is the graph of a function of \(x\), which models the height of a skateboard ramp. The function meets the following requirements.
\begin{itemize}
\item[(i)] At \(x=0\), the value of the function is 0 , and the slope of the graph of the function is 0 .
\item[(ii)] At \(x=4\), the value of the function is 1, and the slope of the graph of the function is 1 .
\item[(iii)] Between \(x=0\) and \(x=4\), the function is increasing.
\end{itemize}
![](https://cdn.mathpix.com/cropped/ae6548c0-b4a7-42c5-9345-285ede81aaad-1.jpg?height=372&width=524&top_left_y=316&top_left_x=1418)
\begin{itemize}
\item[(a)] Let \(f(x)=a x^{2}\), where \(a\) is a nonzero constant. Show that it is not possible to find a value for \(a\) so that \(f\) meets requirement (ii) above.
\item[(b)] Let \(g(x)=c x^{3}-\frac{x^{2}}{16}\), where \(c\) is a nonzero constant. Find the value of \(c\) so that \(g\) meets requirement (ii) above. Show the work that leads to your answer.
\item[(c)] Using the function \(g\) and your value of \(c\) from part (b), show that \(g\) does not meet requirement (iii) above.
\item[(d)] Let \(h(x)=\frac{x^{n}}{k}\), where \(k\) is a nonzero constant and \(n\) is a positive integer. Find the values of \(k\) and \(n\) so that \(h\) meets requirement (ii) above. Show that \(h\) also meets requirements (i) and (iii) above.
\item[(a)] \(f(4)=1\) implies that \(a=\frac{1}{16}\) and \(f^{\prime}(4)=2 a(4)=1\) implies that \(a=\frac{1}{8}\). Thus, \(f\) cannot satisfy (ii).
\item[(b)] \(\quad g(4)=64 c-1=1\) implies that \(c=\frac{1}{32}\). When \(c=\frac{1}{32}, g^{\prime}(4)=3 c(4)^{2}-\frac{2(4)}{16}=3\left(\frac{1}{32}\right)(16)-\frac{1}{2}=1\)
\item[(c)] \(\quad g^{\prime}(x)=\frac{3}{32} x^{2}-\frac{x}{8}=\frac{1}{32} x(3 x-4)\) \(g^{\prime}(x)<0\) for \(0<x<\frac{4}{3}\), so \(g\) does not satisfy (iii).
\item[(d)] \(h(4)=\frac{4^{n}}{k}=1\) implies that \(4^{n}=k\). \(h^{\prime}(4)=\frac{n 4^{n-1}}{k}=\frac{n 4^{n-1}}{4^{n}}=\frac{n}{4}=1\) gives \(n=4\) and \(k=4^{4}=256\). \(h(x)=\frac{x^{4}}{256} \Rightarrow h(0)=0\). \(h^{\prime}(x)=\frac{4 x^{3}}{256} \Rightarrow h^{\prime}(0)=0\) and \(h^{\prime}(x)>0\) for \(0<x<4\).
\end{itemize}
